lessons.title: The anemia workup, run as an algorithm
lessons.body:
## Two questions, in this order

Anemia is a hemoglobin under `13.5 g/dL` in men or `12 g/dL` in women. Once you have that, stop reaching for diagnoses and ask two questions in sequence.

**Question one: is the marrow responding?** Order a **reticulocyte count**. Reticulocytes are red cells released early, so they measure production effort. An absolute reticulocyte count above about `100,000/microliter` (or a reticulocyte production index above `2`) means the marrow is working hard — so the problem is **destruction or loss**. A low count means **underproduction**.

**Question two: what size are the cells?** The mean corpuscular volume splits underproduction into three lanes.

> **Key:** Retic first, MCV second. Running the MCV alone makes you miss hemolysis, which can present with any cell size.

### Lane 1: microcytic, MCV under `80 fL`

| | Iron deficiency | Thalassemia trait | Anemia of chronic disease |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ferritin | low, under `30 ng/mL` is diagnostic | normal | normal or high |
| Total iron binding capacity | high | normal | low |
| Transferrin saturation | under `20%` | normal | low-normal |
| Red cell count | low | normal or high | low |
| RDW (size variation) | high | normal | normal |

The red cell count is the fast discriminator: a patient with small cells and a **normal or high** red cell count has thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency, and giving them iron does nothing but load them with iron.

> **On the exam:** Iron deficiency in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman means endoscopy of both ends of the gut, not an iron prescription. Assume a gastrointestinal cancer until the scopes say otherwise.

### Lane 2: macrocytic, MCV above `100 fL`

Split it into megaloblastic and non-megaloblastic.

**Megaloblastic** means DNA synthesis is blocked — B12 or folate deficiency — and the smear shows **hypersegmented neutrophils**. Separate the two with metabolites: methylmalonic acid is raised in B12 deficiency only, while homocysteine rises in both. That matters because B12 deficiency also damages the spinal cord, and giving folate alone corrects the blood count while the neurologic damage keeps progressing.

**Non-megaloblastic** macrocytosis: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic syndrome, and drugs such as hydroxyurea or zidovudine.

### Lane 3: normocytic

Acute blood loss, anemia of chronic disease, chronic kidney disease (no erythropoietin), early marrow failure — and hemolysis, which usually sits here.

### Proving hemolysis and naming it

Four labs make the case: **high reticulocytes, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin**. Then two tests name the mechanism.

1. **Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.** Positive means antibody-mediated: autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a drug, or a transfusion reaction.
2. **The smear**, if Coombs is negative. Schistocytes (fragmented cells) mean the red cells are being sheared — microangiopathy such as TTP, HUS or DIC, or a mechanical heart valve. Spherocytes mean hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis. Bite cells and Heinz bodies mean G6PD deficiency after an oxidative trigger. Sickle forms speak for themselves.

> **Trap:** Schistocytes with a low platelet count is not a lab curiosity. That combination is TTP, HUS or DIC until proven otherwise, and one of those needs plasma exchange today.

### When to transfuse

In a stable, non-bleeding patient the threshold is a hemoglobin of `7 g/dL`, or `8 g/dL` with acute coronary syndrome. Symptoms and the rate of fall matter more than the number: a chronic `7` may walk in, while a fall to `9` over an hour may be shocked.
keyPoints: Reticulocyte count first: high means destruction or loss, low means underproduction. Then use the MCV.
Iron deficiency has low ferritin, high TIBC and a high RDW; thalassemia trait has a normal or high red cell count.
B12 and folate both cause megaloblastic anemia, but only B12 raises methylmalonic acid and damages the cord.
Hemolysis is high retic, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin; Coombs then smear names the mechanism.
Schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia means TTP, HUS or DIC until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A patient has a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, a red cell count of 5.9 million/microliter and a normal RDW. What is most likely?
checks.why: Small cells with a normal or high red cell count and a normal RDW point to thalassemia trait. Iron deficiency lowers the red cell count and widens the RDW, and giving iron here would only cause overload.

checks.q: A patient with macrocytic anemia has a raised homocysteine but a normal methylmalonic acid. Which deficiency is present?
checks.why: Folate deficiency raises homocysteine alone, while B12 deficiency raises both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. The distinction matters because B12 deficiency causes irreversible neurologic injury.

checks.q: Which laboratory pattern best confirms hemolysis?
choices: Low retic, low LDH, high haptoglobin
High retic, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin
checks.why: Destruction releases LDH and unconjugated bilirubin, consumes haptoglobin, and drives the marrow to release reticulocytes. The other patterns describe chronic disease and iron deficiency.

lessons.title: Bleeding disorders: hemophilia, von Willebrand, ITP, TTP and DIC
lessons.body:
## The bleeding pattern tells you which half of hemostasis failed

**Platelet-type bleeding** is mucocutaneous and immediate: petechiae, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, prolonged oozing from small cuts. That means a platelet problem or von Willebrand disease.

**Factor-type bleeding** is deep and delayed: bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis), muscle hematomas, bleeding that stops and then restarts hours later. That means the coagulation cascade.

> **Key:** Petechiae are a platelet finding. A patient bleeding into a knee is a factor problem. The story sorts the workup before any lab returns.

### Hemophilia A and B

X-linked recessive, so almost always male. Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency (about `80%`), hemophilia B is factor IX. The **PTT is prolonged and the PT is normal**, because both factors sit in the intrinsic pathway.

Severity follows the factor level: under `1%` is severe with spontaneous hemarthroses, `1-5%` moderate, `5-40%` mild with bleeding only after trauma or surgery.

> **Trap:** A hemophiliac with a head injury gets **factor concentrate first, before imaging and before the neurologic exam is repeated**. Waiting for the CT to prove a bleed wastes the only hour that matters.

Mild hemophilia A can be treated with desmopressin, which releases stored factor VIII. Hemophilia B does not respond to it.

### Von Willebrand disease

The most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting roughly `1%` of people, and autosomal rather than X-linked, so women are affected equally — often presenting as lifelong heavy menstrual bleeding. Von Willebrand factor does two jobs: it glues platelets to collagen and it chaperones factor VIII, so the PTT can be mildly prolonged.

Treatment is desmopressin for type 1, or a von Willebrand factor-containing concentrate for severe disease and surgery. Aspirin and NSAIDs are avoided.

### Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

Antibody-coated platelets are destroyed in the spleen. The defining feature is an **isolated** low platelet count: hemoglobin, white count and smear are otherwise normal. In children it typically follows a virus and resolves; in adults it is usually chronic.

Treat only for bleeding or a platelet count under about `20,000-30,000/microliter`: corticosteroids, or intravenous immune globulin when a fast rise is needed. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding because transfused platelets are destroyed just as quickly.

### TTP and HUS: the ones that look similar and are not

**Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)** is a deficiency of ADAMTS13, the enzyme that trims von Willebrand factor. Untrimmed multimers grab platelets and build microthrombi throughout small vessels. The classic pentad is fever, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, kidney injury and neurologic changes — but you only need the **hemolytic anemia with schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia** to act. PT and PTT are normal, which separates it from DIC.

**Treatment is urgent plasma exchange**, plus corticosteroids, and untreated mortality exceeds `90%`.

> **Trap:** Never transfuse platelets in TTP for a low count alone. You are feeding the microthrombi. The same caution applies to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

**Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)** follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli `O157:H7`, usually in a child days after bloody diarrhea, with kidney failure dominating. Care is supportive; antibiotics and antimotility agents may worsen it.

### DIC, managed

Treat the trigger — sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe, malignancy — because nothing else works until it is controlled. Then replace what the patient is losing, **only if bleeding or before a procedure**: platelets to keep the count above `50,000`, fresh frozen plasma for a prolonged PT and PTT, and cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen falls below `150 mg/dL`. Heparin is reserved for the thrombosis-dominant forms.

### Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

A platelet fall of more than `50%` at day `5-10` of heparin, in a patient who is clotting rather than bleeding. Stop all heparin including flushes, start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, and do not give platelets.
keyPoints: Mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae is platelet or von Willebrand; deep joint and muscle bleeding is a factor problem.
Hemophilia prolongs the PTT with a normal PT; a hemophiliac with a head strike gets factor before imaging.
Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and often shows as lifelong heavy periods.
TTP is schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia with normal PT and PTT, treated by urgent plasma exchange, never platelets.
In DIC treat the trigger first, then replace platelets above 50,000, plasma, and cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 150.

checks.q: A 30-year-old woman has a platelet count of 18,000/microliter with a normal hemoglobin, white count and smear, and no schistocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
checks.why: An isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal count and smear is ITP. TTP would show schistocytes and anemia, DIC would prolong the PT and PTT, and hemophilia does not lower platelets.

checks.q: A patient has schistocytes, platelets of 14,000, a creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL, confusion, and a normal PT and PTT. What is the priority?
checks.why: This is TTP, and plasma exchange is the treatment that changes mortality from over 90% to survivable. Platelets fuel the microthrombi, and normal coagulation times argue against DIC.

lessons.title: Transfusion, second pass: massive transfusion, reactions and refusing blood
lessons.body:
## When the bleeding outruns the replacing

### Activating massive transfusion

A massive transfusion protocol replaces `10 units` in 24 hours or `4 units` in an hour, but the point of a protocol is to start it before you can prove the patient meets the definition. Triggers used at the bedside: persistent hypotension with ongoing hemorrhage, a **shock index** (heart rate divided by systolic pressure) above `1`, or a scoring tool such as ABC in trauma.

Give **red cells, plasma and platelets in a `1:1:1` ratio**, which approximates whole blood instead of diluting clotting factors away with red cells alone.

### The four things that kill during a massive transfusion

1. **Hypothermia.** Clotting enzymes are temperature-dependent and stop working at low temperatures. Use a fluid warmer, warm the room, and cover the patient.
2. **Acidosis.** Poor perfusion drives lactate, and acidosis cripples the same enzymes. The fix is stopping the bleeding, not bicarbonate.
3. **Coagulopathy.** Both of the above, plus consumption and dilution.
4. **Hypocalcemia.** Stored blood is anticoagulated with **citrate**, which binds ionized calcium. Rapid transfusion drops ionized calcium, which worsens coagulopathy and drops cardiac contractility and vascular tone. Monitor ionized calcium and replace it during heavy transfusion.

> **Key:** The old lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy is now taught as a diamond, because hypocalcemia belongs in it. Every few units, someone should be asking about calcium and temperature.

**Tranexamic acid** `1 g` over 10 minutes then `1 g` over 8 hours reduces mortality in trauma and in postpartum hemorrhage when given within `3 hours` of injury or delivery. Given later it does not help. Limit crystalloid, which dilutes and cools.

### Reactions, managed rather than just recognized

The first five actions are identical for every suspected reaction: **stop the transfusion, keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing, recheck the patient identifiers against the unit, examine and support the patient, and notify the blood bank**, returning the unit and fresh samples.

After that, the management diverges.

| Reaction | What to do next |
|---|---|
| Febrile non-hemolytic | antipyretic; future leukoreduced products prevent recurrence |
| Mild allergic, hives only | antihistamine; this is the one reaction that may be cautiously restarted if symptoms resolve |
| Anaphylaxis, consider IgA deficiency | epinephrine `0.3 mg` IM, airway support, and washed products in future |
| Acute hemolytic | aggressive isotonic fluids to protect the kidneys, support blood pressure, watch for DIC; this is usually an identification error |
| TRALI | supportive oxygen and ventilation; diuretics do not help because the problem is leaky capillaries, not volume |
| TACO | sit the patient up, give a diuretic, and transfuse future units slowly in split volumes |
| Delayed hemolytic, `3-14 days` later | usually mild: an unexpectedly falling hemoglobin with a new antibody; document the antibody permanently |

> **On shift:** Bacterial contamination, most often of platelets which are stored at room temperature, is now a more likely infectious hazard than viral transmission. HIV and hepatitis C transmission each run around `1 in a million` units or less.

### When the patient declines blood

A competent adult may refuse any transfusion, including one that is life-saving, and that refusal is binding regardless of anyone's opinion of the reason. The work is to make the refusal specific and useful rather than treating it as an all-or-nothing stop.

Many patients who decline whole blood components will accept **albumin, clotting factor concentrates, prothrombin complex concentrate, cryoprecipitate, or intraoperative cell salvage** — these are individual decisions, so ask about each rather than assuming. Document exactly what is accepted and refused, and involve the patient early rather than at the moment of crisis.

Bloodless alternatives to raise or preserve the count: intravenous iron, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, tranexamic acid, early surgical or endoscopic control of bleeding, minimizing phlebotomy volumes with pediatric tubes, and tolerating a lower hemoglobin with oxygen support.

Children are the exception that changes the process: parental refusal for a minor in a life-threatening emergency is handled through the hospital's legal and ethics pathway, and emergency treatment is not delayed while it runs.
keyPoints: Activate massive transfusion on clinical triggers such as a shock index above 1 rather than waiting to meet the definition.
Give 1:1:1 red cells, plasma and platelets, and give tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury or delivery.
The killing diamond is hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and citrate-induced hypocalcemia.
Every reaction starts the same way: stop, saline through new tubing, recheck identifiers, support, notify the blood bank.
A competent adult's refusal of blood is binding; ask component by component and use iron, TXA and cell salvage.

checks.q: During rapid transfusion of 6 units, a patient becomes hypotensive with perioral tingling and a prolonged QT. What is the most likely cause?
checks.why: Citrate in stored blood binds ionized calcium, and rapid transfusion drops it fast enough to cause tingling, QT prolongation and reduced contractility. A hemolytic reaction would bring fever, back pain and dark urine.

checks.q: A patient becomes hypoxic with bilateral infiltrates 3 hours into a transfusion, with a blood pressure of 92/56 and flat neck veins. What should not be done?
choices: Give supplemental oxygen and support ventilation
Give furosemide to clear the infiltrates
Notify the blood bank and return the unit
checks.why: This picture is TRALI, which is capillary leak rather than volume overload, so diuretics do not help and may worsen perfusion. TACO is the one with hypertension and distended neck veins that responds to a diuretic.

lessons.title: HIV, prophylaxis and the adult vaccine schedule
lessons.body:
## Testing, and the window that fools people

The standard screen is a **fourth-generation antigen-antibody combination test**, which detects the p24 antigen as well as antibody and turns positive roughly `18-45 days` after exposure. A nucleic acid test detects virus earliest, from about `10 days`. A reactive screen goes to an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay, and if that is indeterminate, to a nucleic acid test.

**Acute retroviral syndrome** is the trap: a mononucleosis-like illness of fever, sore throat, rash and lymphadenopathy `2-4 weeks` after exposure, at a moment when the viral load is enormous and transmission risk is highest — and antibody may still be negative. If you suspect it, the right order is an HIV RNA test, not a repeat antibody test.

> **Trap:** A negative antibody test in the first few weeks does not exclude HIV. It may mean the patient is at their most infectious point.

### Treatment in one paragraph

Antiretroviral therapy is started the day of diagnosis. The standard regimen is **two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase strand transfer inhibitor** such as bictegravir or dolutegravir, often as one daily pill. The goal is an undetectable viral load, and **undetectable equals untransmittable** for sexual transmission. Adherence is everything, because intermittent dosing breeds resistance. In advanced disease, the first weeks of therapy can bring **immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome**, where a recovering immune system inflames a previously silent infection and the patient appears to get worse while actually improving.

### Opportunistic infections and the thresholds that prevent them

| CD4 count | Infection to expect | Prophylaxis |
|---|---|---|
| `200-500` | thrush, shingles, bacterial pneumonia | none specific |
| under `200` | Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia | trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily |
| under `100` | toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis | the same TMP-SMX covers toxoplasmosis if IgG positive |
| under `50` | CMV retinitis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium | start effective antiretroviral therapy promptly |

### Prophylaxis after and before exposure

**Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)** is started as soon as possible and **within `72 hours`**, and runs `28 days`, typically tenofovir-emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor. Baseline HIV testing is done but treatment is not delayed for it. Hepatitis B status is checked in the same breath.

**Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)** is daily tenofovir-emtricitabine, over `99%` effective against sexual acquisition when taken consistently, or long-acting injectable cabotegravir. It requires a negative HIV test before starting and testing every `3 months`, because starting PrEP during undiagnosed acute infection breeds resistance.

**Occupational needlestick risk** per hollow-bore exposure from an infected source: HIV about `0.3%`, hepatitis C about `1.8%`, and hepatitis B up to `30%` in an unvaccinated worker. Wash, report immediately, and let occupational health test the source.

### The adult vaccine schedule, compressed

| Vaccine | Adult rule |
|---|---|
| Influenza | every year, everyone `6 months` and older |
| COVID-19 | per the current season's recommendation |
| Tdap and Td | one Tdap, then a booster every `10 years`; Tdap in **every** pregnancy at `27-36 weeks` |
| HPV | routine through age `26`, shared decision to `45` |
| Zoster, recombinant | 2 doses from age `50`, and from `19` if immunocompromised |
| Pneumococcal | from age `50`, or younger with risk conditions |
| Hepatitis B | all adults `19-59`, and older with risk factors |
| MMR and varicella | if not immune, and **live**, so not in pregnancy |

**Live vaccines** — MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, yellow fever — are contraindicated in pregnancy and in significant immunosuppression, including a CD4 count under `200`.

> **On the exam:** Tetanus wound management is a two-column question. A clean minor wound needs a booster only if the last dose was over `10 years` ago. A dirty or contaminated wound needs one if it has been over `5 years`, plus tetanus immune globulin when the patient has had fewer than three lifetime doses or the history is unknown.
keyPoints: Fourth-generation antigen-antibody testing turns positive at 18-45 days; suspected acute HIV needs an RNA test, not another antibody test.
Treatment is two NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor started the day of diagnosis, and undetectable equals untransmittable.
TMP-SMX prophylaxis starts at a CD4 under 200 for Pneumocystis and covers toxoplasmosis under 100.
PEP within 72 hours for 28 days; PrEP is over 99% effective with adherence and needs HIV testing every 3 months.
Live vaccines are out in pregnancy and with a CD4 under 200; dirty wounds need a tetanus booster at 5 years, clean ones at 10.

checks.q: A patient has fever, sore throat, rash and lymphadenopathy 18 days after a high-risk exposure. The fourth-generation screen is negative. What is the next test?
choices: Repeat the antibody test in 3 months
checks.why: This is acute retroviral syndrome, when the viral load is enormous but antibodies may not have formed. The RNA test detects virus earliest, and a CD4 count neither diagnoses nor excludes acute infection.

checks.q: A healthcare worker sustains a hollow-bore needlestick from an HIV-positive source 5 hours ago. What is correct?
choices: Start a 28-day PEP regimen now, within the 72-hour window
Wait for the worker's baseline HIV test to return before starting
PEP is only indicated for sexual exposure
Give a single dose of tenofovir-emtricitabine
checks.why: PEP should start as early as possible and within 72 hours, and runs a full 28 days. Baseline testing is drawn but never delays the first dose, and a single dose is not prophylaxis.

checks.q: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks of pregnancy asks which vaccines she should receive.
choices: MMR now, since she is not immune
Tdap in this pregnancy, plus inactivated influenza vaccine
Varicella vaccine to protect the newborn
checks.why: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy at 27-36 weeks to pass antibody to the newborn, and inactivated influenza vaccine is safe. MMR, varicella and the intranasal influenza vaccine are live and contraindicated in pregnancy.

lessons.title: Autoimmune disease at recognition level
lessons.body:
## Learn the opening picture, not the whole textbook

You do not need to manage these diseases. You need to recognize them fast enough to escalate, and to know which ones have an emergency hiding inside.

### Systemic lupus erythematosus

A young woman, most often, with a multisystem illness that comes in flares: a **malar rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose that spares the nasolabial folds**, photosensitivity, painless oral ulcers, non-erosive joint pain, serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis), kidney involvement with proteinuria, and cytopenias.

Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is positive in nearly everyone with lupus, which makes it sensitive and nearly useless for confirmation — plenty of healthy people are ANA positive. **Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are the specific ones**, and falling complement (C3, C4) with rising anti-dsDNA suggests an active flare.

Drug-induced lupus, classically from hydralazine, procainamide or isoniazid, spares the kidneys and brain and resolves when the drug stops.

### Rheumatoid arthritis

**Symmetric** small joint arthritis of the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists, with morning stiffness lasting **over an hour**, improving with use. It is erosive — it destroys joints — which is why early treatment matters. Rheumatoid factor is sensitive, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide is specific.

> **Key:** Rheumatoid arthritis spares the distal interphalangeal joints. Distal joint involvement points to osteoarthritis or psoriatic arthritis instead.

> **Trap:** Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis erodes the cervical spine and can produce **atlantoaxial instability**. That is a real hazard during intubation or any neck manipulation.

### Ankylosing spondylitis

A young man with **inflammatory** back pain: worse with rest, better with exercise, waking him in the second half of the night, with more than `30 minutes` of morning stiffness. Over years the sacroiliac joints and spine fuse, chest expansion falls, and posture becomes stooped. HLA-B27 is associated, and anterior uveitis is the classic extra-articular finding.

A fused spine behaves like a long bone: it fractures with trivial trauma, often in the cervical spine, and those fractures are unstable. Anyone with ankylosing spondylitis and new neck pain after a minor fall needs imaging.

### Vasculitis, sorted by vessel size

**Giant cell (temporal) arteritis** is the one to know cold. Age over `50`, a new headache, scalp tenderness, **jaw claudication** (pain while chewing), and visual loss. ESR and CRP are markedly raised. It overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica, which causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness.

> **On shift:** Start high-dose corticosteroids **immediately** on suspicion of giant cell arteritis. Vision loss is sudden and permanent, and the temporal artery biopsy stays positive for about two weeks after steroids begin, so treating first costs nothing diagnostically.

**ANCA-associated vasculitis**, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, hits the upper airway (chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting), the lungs (nodules, hemoptysis) and the kidneys (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis) together. That triad in one patient is the pattern.

**IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura)** is a child with **palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs**, abdominal pain, joint pain and hematuria after a viral illness.

### The rest, in one line each

- **Sjogren syndrome**: dry eyes and dry mouth, anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, and dental decay from the dryness.
- **Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)**: tight thickened skin, Raynaud phenomenon, reflux — with **scleroderma renal crisis**, a hypertensive emergency treated specifically with an ACE inhibitor.
- **Antiphospholipid syndrome**: arterial and venous clots plus recurrent pregnancy loss, and paradoxically a **prolonged PTT** in a patient who clots.

> **Key:** The common thread is treatment. These patients live on immunosuppression, which blunts fever, masks peritonitis and turns ordinary infections dangerous.
keyPoints: ANA is sensitive and non-specific in lupus; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific antibodies, and falling complement suggests a flare.
Rheumatoid arthritis is symmetric, erosive, spares the DIP joints, and can cause atlantoaxial instability.
Ankylosing spondylitis is inflammatory back pain better with exercise; a fused spine fractures with minor trauma.
Giant cell arteritis: over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, high ESR — start steroids before the biopsy to save vision.
Immunosuppression is the shared hazard: blunted fever, masked peritonitis, and ordinary infections turning severe.

checks.q: A 68-year-old has 3 weeks of new temporal headache, pain in the jaw while chewing, and an ESR of 96 mm/hr. What is the correct first action?
choices: Arrange temporal artery biopsy and treat based on the result
Start an NSAID and reassess in a week
Obtain a head CT before any treatment
checks.why: Vision loss in giant cell arteritis is sudden and irreversible, and the biopsy remains positive for roughly two weeks after steroids start. Waiting for tissue confirmation risks blindness for no diagnostic gain.

checks.q: Which feature argues against rheumatoid arthritis?
checks.why: Rheumatoid arthritis characteristically spares the DIP joints, which are the hallmark of osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis. The other three features are typical of rheumatoid disease.

lessons.title: Oncology basics and the oncologic emergencies
lessons.body:
## Enough cancer to be useful at the bedside

### The common ones

By new cases: **breast** in women, **prostate** in men, then **lung** and **colorectal** in both. By deaths, **lung cancer** leads by a wide margin, because it is usually found late.

Screening, in broad strokes: mammography beginning in the forties, colorectal screening from age `45`, cervical cytology from `21`, low-dose chest CT for adults `50-80` with a `20 pack-year` smoking history, and prostate testing by shared decision from `55-69`. Exact ages vary by guideline and are revised often.

### Staging versus grading

**Stage** is how far the cancer has spread and it drives prognosis and treatment. The **TNM** system reads tumor size or depth, nodal involvement, and distant metastasis, and those combine into stages I through IV. **Grade** is a different question — how abnormal the cells look under the microscope, from well differentiated to poorly differentiated.

> **Key:** Stage answers how far. Grade answers how ugly. A high-grade stage I tumor and a low-grade stage IV tumor are completely different conversations.

### The treatments and the trouble each brings

- **Surgery** removes local disease.
- **Radiation** treats a field, with skin changes, fatigue, and organ-specific injury such as mucositis or pneumonitis.
- **Cytotoxic chemotherapy** kills dividing cells, which is why it also hits marrow (neutropenia at the nadir `7-14 days`), gut lining (mucositis, diarrhea), and hair follicles.
- **Targeted and hormonal therapy** attacks a specific receptor or pathway.
- **Immunotherapy**, particularly checkpoint inhibitors, releases the brakes on T cells. The side effects are autoimmune: colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis, dermatitis, hypophysitis — and they are treated with corticosteroids, not with antibiotics.

### The emergencies, with what to do

**Febrile neutropenia** — covered earlier, and still the most common: cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour.

**Tumor lysis syndrome.** Dying tumor cells spill their contents `12-72 hours` after treatment starts, most often in bulky, rapidly dividing cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma. The panel is **high potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid and low calcium**, with acute kidney injury following. Prevention is aggressive hydration plus allopurinol, or rasburicase in high-risk patients. Do not reflexively replace the calcium — with the phosphate that high, giving calcium risks precipitation in tissue.

**Malignant spinal cord compression.** Back pain that is worse at night and when lying flat, present for weeks, then weakness, then a sensory level, and finally bladder and bowel dysfunction. **Give dexamethasone immediately and get urgent MRI of the whole spine**, because a second, silent lesion is common. Neurologic status at the moment of treatment is the best predictor of whether the patient walks again.

**Superior vena cava syndrome.** Facial and arm swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins, headache, worse when lying flat or bending forward. Elevate the head, and treat the tumor with radiation, chemotherapy or a stent. The true emergency is airway edema or cerebral edema, not the cosmetic swelling.

**Hypercalcemia of malignancy.** Confusion, constipation, dehydration and a shortened QT. Isotonic saline first, calcitonin for a rapid but short-lived drop, and a bisphosphonate for durable control.

**Hyperviscosity syndrome.** Very high paraprotein or blast counts thicken the blood: blurred vision, headache, mucosal bleeding, confusion. Treated by plasmapheresis or leukapheresis.

> **On shift:** New back pain in a patient with known cancer is a cord compression until imaging says otherwise. The window between pain and permanent paralysis can be days, and the pain is often dismissed as musculoskeletal.
keyPoints: Lung cancer kills the most; breast, prostate, lung and colorectal are the most common diagnoses.
Stage is how far it has spread by TNM; grade is how abnormal the cells look.
Checkpoint inhibitor side effects are autoimmune — colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis — and are treated with steroids.
Tumor lysis is high potassium, phosphate and uric acid with low calcium, 12-72 hours after therapy starts.
New back pain in a cancer patient is cord compression until proven otherwise: dexamethasone now, then urgent whole-spine MRI.

checks.q: Two days after starting chemotherapy for a bulky lymphoma, a patient has potassium 6.4 mEq/L, phosphate 7.8 mg/dL, uric acid 12 mg/dL, calcium 7.0 mg/dL and a creatinine that has doubled. What is this?
checks.why: Cells dying en masse release potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids that become uric acid, while phosphate binds calcium and lowers it. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is the opposite calcium picture.

checks.q: A patient with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of worsening back pain, now with leg weakness and difficulty urinating. What is the best first step?
choices: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine
Dexamethasone now and urgent MRI of the entire spine
CT of the lumbar spine without contrast
checks.why: Steroids reduce cord edema while imaging is arranged, and the whole spine is imaged because a second compressive lesion is common. Plain films and non-contrast CT cannot exclude cord compression.

lessons.title: The rash approach: twenty rashes, skin cancer and drug eruptions
lessons.body:
## Four questions before you name anything

1. **Is the patient sick?** Fever, hypotension, mucous membrane involvement, or pain out of proportion to what you see. That question alone separates the rashes that kill from the rashes that itch.
2. **Does it blanch?** Press with a glass or a fingertip. Blanching means blood still inside vessels. **Non-blanching means blood outside vessels** — petechiae or purpura.
3. **What is the primary lesion?** Flat and under `1 cm` is a macule, raised and small is a papule, a broad raised area is a plaque, fluid-filled and small is a vesicle, large is a bulla, pus-filled is a pustule, transient and edematous is a wheal.
4. **Where is it, and how is it distributed?** Dermatomal, flexural, sun-exposed, palms and soles, mucosal.

> **Key:** Five red flags mean stop and escalate: non-blanching rash with fever, mucous membrane involvement, skin that is painful to touch, skin that sloughs, and anything spreading over hours.

### Twenty rashes, described in words

| What you see | What it is |
|---|---|
| Non-blanching petechiae and purpura in an ill febrile patient | meningococcemia until proven otherwise |
| Spots starting on wrists and ankles moving inward, after a tick bite | Rocky Mountain spotted fever |
| Painful dusky skin sloughing in sheets with eroded lips and eyes | Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis |
| Fever, facial swelling, widespread rash and eosinophilia weeks into a new drug | DRESS |
| Dozens of tiny sterile pustules on red skin days into an antibiotic | acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis |
| Raised blanching wheals that move and fade within hours | urticaria, a type I reaction |
| Pink blanching macules and papules starting on the trunk a week into a drug | morbilliform drug eruption |
| An expanding round red patch, sometimes clearing centrally, after a tick | erythema migrans of early Lyme disease |
| Grouped painful vesicles in one dermatome stopping at the midline | shingles |
| Crops of vesicles at different stages, trunk to face, in a child | chickenpox |
| Vesicles on palms, soles and in the mouth of a toddler | hand, foot and mouth disease |
| Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, white spots in the mouth, then a rash from the face down | measles |
| Diffuse sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue after sore throat | scarlet fever |
| Sunburn-like rash with hypotension, then peeling of palms after `1-2 weeks` | toxic shock syndrome |
| Sharply demarcated bright red raised plaque on the face or shin | erysipelas |
| Warm, tender, spreading redness with no sharp edge and no drainable pocket | cellulitis |
| Skin barely red but agonizing pain, crepitus and a toxic patient | necrotizing fasciitis |
| Itchy linear vesicles where a plant or nickel touched skin, `48-72 hours` later | allergic contact dermatitis |
| Silvery scaling plaques on elbows, knees and scalp, with pitted nails | psoriasis |
| Intense night itching with burrows in finger webs, wrists and waistline | scabies |

### Skin cancer, recognized

**ABCDE** for melanoma: **A**symmetry, **B**order irregularity, **C**olor variation, **D**iameter over `6 mm`, **E**volving. Add the ugly duckling rule — the mole that does not look like the patient's other moles.

- **Basal cell carcinoma**: a pearly, translucent papule with fine surface vessels and a rolled edge, on sun-exposed skin, sometimes ulcerated centrally. Locally destructive, almost never metastasizes.
- **Squamous cell carcinoma**: a firm scaly or ulcerated nodule, often on the lip, ear or in an old scar or chronic wound. It can metastasize.
- **Melanoma**: the deadly one, and prognosis follows depth. **Acral lentiginous melanoma** appears on palms, soles and under nails and is the form most often missed in darker skin, where it is proportionally more common.

### Drug eruptions, timed

Timing narrows the list better than appearance. Urticaria arrives within minutes to hours. A morbilliform eruption comes at `4-14 days`. Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis start at `4-28 days`. DRESS is late, at `2-8 weeks`. AGEP is fast, at `1-3 days`.

The usual culprits are sulfonamide antibiotics, penicillins, anticonvulsants such as lamotrigine, carbamazepine and phenytoin, allopurinol, and NSAIDs.

> **Trap:** A positive Nikolsky sign — gentle lateral pressure shears the top layer of skin away — belongs to toxic epidermal necrolysis, pemphigus vulgaris and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. It means the skin is failing as an organ, and that patient belongs in a burn unit.
keyPoints: Ask four questions: is the patient sick, does it blanch, what is the primary lesion, and where is it distributed.
Red flags: non-blanching with fever, mucosal involvement, painful skin, sloughing skin, and spread over hours.
ABCDE plus the ugly duckling rule for melanoma; acral lentiginous melanoma on palms, soles and nails is the one most missed.
Drug eruption timing: urticaria in hours, morbilliform 4-14 days, SJS and TEN 4-28 days, DRESS 2-8 weeks, AGEP 1-3 days.
A positive Nikolsky sign means TEN, pemphigus vulgaris or staph scalded skin, and burn-unit level care.

checks.q: A 19-year-old has a temperature of 39.4 C, a blood pressure of 88/50 and scattered purple spots on the legs that do not blanch. What is the immediate concern?
checks.why: A non-blanching rash in a febrile, hypotensive patient means blood outside the vessels from a disseminated infection until proven otherwise. Urticarial and eczematous rashes blanch and do not cause shock.

checks.q: A patient started lamotrigine 5 weeks ago and now has fever, facial swelling, a widespread rash, transaminitis and an eosinophil count of 1,800. Which reaction is this?
checks.why: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is the late one at 2-8 weeks, with fever, facial edema, eosinophilia and organ involvement. A simple morbilliform eruption has no fever, eosinophilia or organ injury.

lessons.title: Pregnancy complications, second pass
lessons.body:
## What goes wrong, trimester by trimester

### Hyperemesis gravidarum

Not ordinary morning sickness: persistent vomiting with **weight loss over `5%`** of pre-pregnancy weight, ketonuria, dehydration and electrolyte derangement, peaking around `9 weeks`. Treat with intravenous fluids and antiemetics in order — pyridoxine with doxylamine first, then metoclopramide, promethazine or ondansetron.

> **Trap:** Give **thiamine before any dextrose-containing fluid** in prolonged vomiting. A glucose load in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, and it has happened in exactly this population.

Unusually severe cases prompt a look for a molar pregnancy or twins, because both produce very high hCG.

### Gestational diabetes

Placental hormones create insulin resistance by design. Screening happens at `24-28 weeks` with a `50 g` glucose challenge and, if abnormal, a `100 g` three-hour tolerance test. Risks are a large baby (macrosomia) with shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia after delivery, preeclampsia and cesarean birth. Treatment starts with diet and glucose monitoring, then insulin. Screen again at `4-12 weeks` postpartum, because roughly half will develop type 2 diabetes within a decade.

### The hypertensive disorders

**Preeclampsia** is new hypertension of `140/90` or higher after `20 weeks` with proteinuria **or** end-organ signs. **Severe features** change everything: systolic `160` or diastolic `110` or higher, platelets under `100,000`, creatinine over `1.1 mg/dL` or doubled, transaminases at twice normal, pulmonary edema, or new headache or visual disturbance. **Eclampsia** is a seizure. **HELLP** is hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, often with right upper quadrant pain.

Management has three parts:

1. **Magnesium sulfate** for seizure prevention and treatment: `4-6 g` IV load over 20 minutes, then `2 g/hr`. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output, because magnesium is cleared by the kidney. Loss of reflexes is the first sign of toxicity; treat with **calcium gluconate `1 g` IV**.
2. **Antihypertensives** for severe-range pressure: labetalol `20 mg` IV, hydralazine `5-10 mg` IV, or immediate-release nifedipine `10 mg` orally. Target `140-150/90-100` — not normal, because placental perfusion depends on pressure.
3. **Delivery** is the only cure.

> **Key:** Preeclampsia and eclampsia can appear for the first time **up to 6 weeks after delivery**. A postpartum woman with a headache and a blood pressure of `168/104` is not a routine visit.

### Bleeding: the placental emergencies

| Problem | Picture |
|---|---|
| Placenta previa | **painless** bright red bleeding, soft uterus; no digital or speculum exam until ultrasound excludes it |
| Placental abruption | **painful** bleeding, rigid tender uterus, fetal distress; bleeding may be concealed, and DIC can follow |
| Uterine rupture | sudden tearing pain, loss of fetal station, fetal bradycardia, usually with a prior cesarean scar |
| Vasa previa | painless bleeding at membrane rupture with rapid fetal deterioration |

### Postpartum hemorrhage

Defined as blood loss over `1000 mL`, or any bleeding with signs of hypovolemia. Causes are the **four Ts**: **Tone** (uterine atony, `70-80%` of cases), **Trauma** (lacerations, uterine inversion), **Tissue** (retained placenta), **Thrombin** (coagulopathy).

The ladder, in order: fundal massage and bladder emptying, **oxytocin** `10-40 units` in `1 L` of crystalloid, **tranexamic acid `1 g`** within `3 hours` of delivery, then **methylergonovine `0.2 mg` IM** — avoided in hypertension — or **carboprost `250 mcg` IM**, avoided in asthma, or misoprostol `800 mcg`. If drugs fail: intrauterine balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolization, then surgery.

### The other postpartum emergencies

**Endometritis**: fever, uterine tenderness and foul lochia days after delivery. **Amniotic fluid embolism**: sudden collapse with hypoxia, cardiovascular failure and DIC during or just after delivery. **Postpartum psychosis**: a psychiatric emergency distinct from postpartum depression, presenting within weeks with delusions or confusion and carrying real risk to mother and infant.
keyPoints: Hyperemesis means over 5% weight loss with ketonuria; give thiamine before any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Gestational diabetes is screened at 24-28 weeks and rescreened 4-12 weeks postpartum because type 2 often follows.
Magnesium 4-6 g load then 2 g/hr for preeclampsia with severe features; lost reflexes mean toxicity, treated with calcium gluconate.
Previa bleeds painlessly with a soft uterus; abruption bleeds painfully with a rigid tender uterus and can cause DIC.
Postpartum hemorrhage is the four Ts, with atony causing 70-80%: massage, oxytocin, TXA within 3 hours, then second-line uterotonics.

checks.q: A woman at 34 weeks has a blood pressure of 168/112, a headache, platelets of 82,000 and an AST of 140 U/L. What is the priority treatment?
choices: Oral labetalol and follow up in a week
Magnesium sulfate load and infusion plus IV antihypertensives
checks.why: These are preeclampsia with severe features plus HELLP-range labs, and magnesium prevents seizures while IV antihypertensives bring severe-range pressures down. Delivery follows, but it is not performed before stabilizing the mother.

checks.q: A woman with asthma has postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony that has not responded to massage and oxytocin. Which uterotonic must be avoided?
checks.why: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that causes bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma, just as methylergonovine is avoided in hypertension. Misoprostol and tranexamic acid are safe choices here.

checks.q: A woman 12 days postpartum arrives with a severe headache and a blood pressure of 172/108. What should be considered?
checks.why: Preeclampsia and eclampsia can present for the first time up to 6 weeks after delivery, and severe-range pressure with a headache is an end-organ warning sign that requires treatment, not reassurance.

lessons.title: Sexual health, second pass: infections, contraception and male emergencies
lessons.body:
## Treating the patient and the people they will see next

### The regimens worth knowing

| Infection | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Chlamydia | doxycycline `100 mg` twice daily for `7 days`; azithromycin `1 g` once in pregnancy |
| Gonorrhea | ceftriaxone `500 mg` IM once, and treat chlamydia unless it has been excluded |
| Syphilis, early | benzathine penicillin G `2.4 million units` IM once; three weekly doses in late latent disease |
| Trichomoniasis | metronidazole `500 mg` twice daily for `7 days` in women, `2 g` once in men |
| Genital herpes | valacyclovir, episodically for outbreaks or daily for suppression |
| Pelvic inflammatory disease | ceftriaxone `500 mg` IM plus doxycycline and metronidazole for `14 days` |

Penicillin is the only adequate treatment for syphilis in pregnancy, so a penicillin-allergic pregnant patient is desensitized rather than given an alternative. Within `24 hours` of treating syphilis, fever, chills and a worsening rash may appear — the **Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction** — which is dying organisms, not an allergy.

### Partners are part of the treatment

An infection treated in one person and not their partner comes straight back. The rules: **abstain from sex for `7 days` after treatment and until partners are treated**, treat partners from the last `60 days`, and retest — not a test of cure, but a **repeat test at `3 months`**, because reinfection is common. Test of cure is reserved for pregnancy and pharyngeal gonorrhea.

**Expedited partner therapy** allows the clinician to provide treatment for a partner who has not been examined, and it is permitted for chlamydia and gonorrhea in most states including New Jersey. Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and HIV are reportable to public health.

> **On shift:** Offer HIV testing and hepatitis screening with any sexually transmitted infection diagnosis, and offer PrEP to anyone whose exposure risk is ongoing.

### Contraception, ranked by how often it actually fails

Typical-use failure over one year: implant and intrauterine devices under `1%`, the injection about `4%`, pill, patch and ring about `7%`, male condoms about `13%`, withdrawal about `20%`. The gap between perfect and typical use is the whole story — long-acting methods win because they do not depend on the user.

Duration: copper IUD `10-12 years`, levonorgestrel IUD `3-8 years` by product, implant `3-5 years`.

**Estrogen is contraindicated** in migraine with aura, a history of venous thromboembolism or known thrombophilia, smoking at age `35` or older, uncontrolled hypertension, current breast cancer, and the first `21 days` postpartum. Progestin-only methods are available in all of those.

### Emergency contraception

Three options, in descending effectiveness:

1. **Copper IUD** — over `99%` effective, up to `5 days` after intercourse, and it stays as ongoing contraception.
2. **Ulipristal acetate `30 mg`** — up to `120 hours`, and it holds its effectiveness better than levonorgestrel late in that window and at higher body weight.
3. **Levonorgestrel `1.5 mg`** — available without prescription, up to `72 hours`, less effective as time passes and above a body mass index of about `26`.

> **Key:** Emergency contraception works primarily by delaying ovulation. It does not end an established pregnancy and is not an abortifacient — a point patients are frequently misinformed about.

### Male genitourinary emergencies, second pass

**Torsion versus epididymitis.** Torsion is sudden and severe, often waking the patient, with a **high-riding testicle in a horizontal lie, an absent cremasteric reflex**, and no relief with elevation. Epididymitis builds over days with fever and dysuria and eases with elevation. Salvage rates approach `90%` inside `6 hours` and fall under `10%` past `24 hours`. If imaging will delay surgery, manual detorsion is attempted by rotating medial to lateral like opening a book — but it never replaces the operating room.

**Ischemic priapism** is a compartment syndrome of the penis: rigid, painful, over `4 hours`, classically in sickle cell disease. It needs aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine urgently. Non-ischemic priapism after trauma is not an emergency.

**Paraphimosis** is a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans, swelling until blood flow is compromised. It needs steady compression and manual reduction now.

**Fournier gangrene** is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, usually in diabetes, with pain out of proportion and crepitus. It is a surgical emergency.

And a non-emergency worth naming: a **painless firm testicular mass** in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise.
keyPoints: Chlamydia is doxycycline for 7 days, gonorrhea is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, and early syphilis is one dose of benzathine penicillin.
Partners from the last 60 days are treated, sex waits 7 days, and retesting happens at 3 months; expedited partner therapy is allowed in New Jersey.
Long-acting methods fail under 1% because they do not depend on the user; estrogen is out with migraine with aura or prior VTE.
Emergency contraception: copper IUD best up to 5 days, ulipristal to 120 hours, levonorgestrel to 72 — all work by delaying ovulation.
Torsion is sudden with an absent cremasteric reflex and a 6-hour window; ischemic priapism, paraphimosis and Fournier gangrene are the other clocks.

checks.q: A 22-year-old is treated for chlamydia. What should she be told about her partner and follow-up?
choices: No partner treatment is needed if he is asymptomatic
Partners from the last 60 days need treatment, abstain 7 days, and retest at 3 months
Return for a test of cure in 1 week
Her partner only needs treatment if she has symptoms again
checks.why: Untreated partners cause rapid reinfection, so partners from the previous 60 days are treated and sex waits 7 days after treatment. Routine test of cure is not recommended outside pregnancy, but retesting at 3 months is.

checks.q: A patient with a body mass index of 34 requests emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected intercourse. Which option is most effective?
checks.why: The copper IUD is over 99% effective up to 5 days and its effectiveness is not reduced by body weight, and it continues as contraception. Levonorgestrel is both time-limited and less effective at higher body mass index.

cards.front: Which test comes first in an anemia workup, and what does it tell you?
cards.back: The reticulocyte count. An absolute count above about 100,000/microliter means the marrow is responding, so the cause is destruction or loss. A low count means underproduction.

cards.front: How do iron studies differ between iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease?
cards.back: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, high TIBC, transferrin saturation under 20%, high RDW. Chronic disease: normal or high ferritin, low TIBC, low-normal saturation, normal RDW.

cards.front: What single count separates thalassemia trait from iron deficiency?
cards.back: The red blood cell count. Thalassemia trait has small cells with a normal or high red cell count and a normal RDW; iron deficiency has a low red cell count and a wide RDW.

cards.front: Which metabolites separate B12 from folate deficiency, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Methylmalonic acid is raised in B12 deficiency only; homocysteine is raised in both. Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient corrects the blood count while neurologic damage progresses.

cards.front: Name the non-megaloblastic causes of macrocytosis.
cards.back: Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic syndrome, and drugs such as hydroxyurea and zidovudine. These lack the hypersegmented neutrophils of B12 or folate deficiency.

cards.front: What does a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test mean in hemolysis?
cards.back: The destruction is antibody-mediated: autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a drug-induced antibody, or a transfusion reaction. A negative test sends you to the smear for a mechanical or intrinsic cause.

cards.front: What does each abnormal red cell shape on a smear suggest?
cards.back: Schistocytes: microangiopathy such as TTP, HUS, DIC or a mechanical valve. Spherocytes: hereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis. Bite cells with Heinz bodies: G6PD deficiency after an oxidant.

cards.front: What does iron deficiency in an adult man or postmenopausal woman require?
cards.back: Endoscopy of the upper and lower gastrointestinal tract. It is a gastrointestinal bleed, often from a cancer, until the scopes prove otherwise — not simply an iron prescription.

cards.front: How does platelet-type bleeding differ from factor-type bleeding?
cards.back: Platelet type is mucocutaneous and immediate: petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy periods. Factor type is deep and delayed: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, and rebleeding hours later.

cards.front: What is the inheritance, factor and lab pattern of hemophilia A and B?
cards.back: Both are X-linked recessive, so almost always male. A is factor VIII deficiency, B is factor IX. PTT is prolonged and PT is normal, because both are intrinsic pathway factors.

cards.front: How is hemophilia severity graded by factor level?
cards.back: Under 1% is severe with spontaneous hemarthroses, 1-5% is moderate with bleeding after minor trauma, and 5-40% is mild with bleeding only after significant trauma or surgery.

cards.front: What is the rule for a hemophiliac with a head injury?
cards.back: Give factor concentrate first, before imaging and before repeating the neurologic exam. Waiting for a CT to prove the bleed wastes the only window that changes the outcome.

cards.front: Why does von Willebrand disease present differently from hemophilia?
cards.back: It is autosomal, so it affects women equally and often shows as lifelong heavy menstrual bleeding. Von Willebrand factor glues platelets to collagen, so bleeding is mucocutaneous, and it also carries factor VIII.

cards.front: What defines immune thrombocytopenia and when is it treated?
cards.back: An isolated low platelet count with an otherwise normal blood count and smear. Treat only for bleeding or a count under about 20,000-30,000, with steroids or IVIG when a fast rise is needed.

cards.front: What is the mechanism, minimum diagnostic finding and treatment of TTP?
cards.back: ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves oversized von Willebrand multimers that trap platelets. You need only microangiopathic hemolysis with schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia to act. Treatment is urgent plasma exchange.

cards.front: Which two conditions forbid platelet transfusion for a low count alone?
cards.back: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Both are clotting disorders that consume platelets, and transfusing feeds the microthrombi.

cards.front: How is DIC managed once the trigger is being treated?
cards.back: Replace only if bleeding or before a procedure: platelets to keep the count above 50,000, fresh frozen plasma for prolonged PT and PTT, and cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 150 mg/dL.

cards.front: How is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia recognized and treated?
cards.back: A platelet fall of more than 50% at day 5-10 of heparin, with clotting rather than bleeding. Stop all heparin including flushes, start argatroban or another non-heparin anticoagulant, and do not transfuse platelets.

cards.front: What bedside triggers activate a massive transfusion protocol?
cards.back: Persistent hypotension with ongoing hemorrhage, a shock index (heart rate divided by systolic pressure) above 1, or a trauma score such as ABC. You activate before the definition is met.

cards.front: Why does rapid transfusion cause hypocalcemia, and what does it do?
cards.back: Stored blood is anticoagulated with citrate, which binds ionized calcium. The resulting low calcium worsens coagulopathy, weakens cardiac contractility and drops vascular tone.

cards.front: What is the modern lethal diamond of massive hemorrhage?
cards.back: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypocalcemia. Warming the patient and fluids, restoring perfusion, replacing 1:1:1 and replacing calcium address all four.

cards.front: What is the tranexamic acid dose and window?
cards.back: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, given within 3 hours of injury or delivery. Given later it does not reduce mortality and may cause harm.

cards.front: What are the first five actions for any suspected transfusion reaction?
cards.back: Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing, recheck patient identifiers against the unit, examine and support the patient, and notify the blood bank with the unit and fresh samples.

cards.front: How does management of TRALI differ from TACO?
cards.back: TRALI is capillary leak: supportive oxygen and ventilation, and diuretics do not help. TACO is volume overload with hypertension and distended neck veins: sit up, diurese, and transfuse future units slowly in split volumes.

cards.front: What is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.back: An unexpected fall in hemoglobin 3-14 days after transfusion as an anamnestic antibody response destroys donor cells. It is usually mild, and the antibody must be documented permanently.

cards.front: Which blood products and alternatives may a patient who declines transfusion still accept?
cards.back: Many accept albumin, clotting factor concentrates, prothrombin complex concentrate, cryoprecipitate or cell salvage. Ask component by component and document exactly what is accepted and refused.

cards.front: What bloodless strategies preserve or raise hemoglobin?
cards.back: Intravenous iron, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, tranexamic acid, prompt surgical or endoscopic control of bleeding, pediatric-volume phlebotomy tubes, and tolerating a lower hemoglobin with oxygen support.

cards.front: When does a fourth-generation HIV test turn positive, and what is the earliest test?
cards.back: The antigen-antibody combination test turns positive at about 18-45 days because it detects p24 antigen. A nucleic acid test detects virus from roughly 10 days.

cards.front: What is acute retroviral syndrome and which test should be ordered?
cards.back: A mononucleosis-like illness 2-4 weeks after exposure, when viral load is enormous and antibody may still be negative. Order an HIV RNA test, not a repeat antibody test.

cards.front: What is a standard first antiretroviral regimen, and what does U equals U mean?
cards.back: Two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase inhibitor such as bictegravir or dolutegravir, started the day of diagnosis. Undetectable viral load equals untransmittable by sex.

cards.front: At which CD4 counts does prophylaxis start, and for what?
cards.back: Under 200: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis. Under 100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG: the same drug covers it. Under 50: prompt effective antiretroviral therapy is the main protection.

cards.front: What is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome?
cards.back: In advanced HIV, a recovering immune system inflames a previously silent infection in the first weeks of antiretroviral therapy, so the patient appears to worsen while actually improving.

cards.front: Give the timing and duration of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.
cards.back: Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours, then continue 28 days, typically tenofovir-emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor. Baseline testing is drawn but never delays the first dose.

cards.front: How effective is PrEP, and what monitoring does it require?
cards.back: Daily tenofovir-emtricitabine is over 99% effective against sexual acquisition when adherent. It requires a negative HIV test before starting and testing every 3 months, plus renal monitoring.

cards.front: What is the per-exposure risk from a hollow-bore needlestick from an infected source?
cards.back: HIV about 0.3%, hepatitis C about 1.8%, and hepatitis B up to 30% in an unvaccinated worker. Wash, report immediately, and have occupational health test the source.

cards.front: Summarize the adult vaccine schedule.
cards.back: Influenza yearly, COVID per season, Tdap once then a booster every 10 years and in every pregnancy at 27-36 weeks, HPV through 26, recombinant zoster from 50, pneumococcal from 50, hepatitis B for all adults 19-59.

cards.front: Which vaccines are live, and what is the tetanus wound rule?
cards.back: Live: MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, yellow fever — avoided in pregnancy and with a CD4 under 200. Clean minor wound: booster if over 10 years. Dirty wound: booster if over 5 years, plus immune globulin if fewer than 3 prior doses.

cards.front: Which lupus antibodies are sensitive and which are specific?
cards.back: ANA is positive in nearly all lupus patients but also in many healthy people, so it is sensitive only. Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith are the specific antibodies.

cards.front: What suggests an active lupus flare on labs, and what causes drug-induced lupus?
cards.back: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement C3 and C4. Drug-induced lupus comes from hydralazine, procainamide or isoniazid, spares kidney and brain, and resolves when the drug stops.

cards.front: Describe the joint pattern of rheumatoid arthritis and what it spares.
cards.back: Symmetric MCP, PIP and wrist involvement with morning stiffness over an hour that improves with use, and it is erosive. It spares the distal interphalangeal joints, which belong to osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis.

cards.front: Why does long-standing rheumatoid arthritis matter before intubation?
cards.back: Chronic inflammation erodes the cervical spine and can cause atlantoaxial instability, so neck manipulation during airway management risks spinal cord injury.

cards.front: What is inflammatory back pain, and why is a fused spine dangerous?
cards.back: Pain worse with rest and better with exercise, waking the patient late at night, with over 30 minutes of morning stiffness. A fused ankylosing spine fractures with trivial trauma, often unstably in the neck.

cards.front: What are the features of giant cell arteritis and why is treatment immediate?
cards.back: Age over 50, new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, very high ESR and CRP. Start high-dose steroids on suspicion: vision loss is permanent and biopsy stays positive for about 2 weeks.

cards.front: Which organ triad suggests ANCA-associated vasculitis, and what is IgA vasculitis?
cards.back: Upper airway with sinusitis and nasal crusting, lungs with nodules or hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. IgA vasculitis is a child with palpable purpura on buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, arthritis and hematuria.

cards.front: Name the key features of Sjogren syndrome, scleroderma and antiphospholipid syndrome.
cards.back: Sjogren: dry eyes and mouth with anti-Ro and anti-La. Scleroderma: thick skin, Raynaud, reflux, and renal crisis treated with an ACE inhibitor. Antiphospholipid: clots plus pregnancy loss with a paradoxically prolonged PTT.

cards.front: Which cancers are most common, and which kills the most?
cards.back: Most new cases: breast in women, prostate in men, then lung and colorectal. Lung cancer causes the most deaths because it is usually found late.

cards.front: What is the difference between stage and grade?
cards.back: Stage is how far the cancer has spread, read by TNM as tumor, nodes and metastasis, and it drives treatment. Grade is how abnormal the cells look microscopically.

cards.front: What kind of side effects do checkpoint inhibitors cause, and how are they treated?
cards.back: Autoimmune ones: colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, pneumonitis, dermatitis and hypophysitis. They are treated with corticosteroids, not antibiotics.

cards.front: Give the laboratory picture and timing of tumor lysis syndrome.
cards.back: High potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid and low calcium with acute kidney injury, 12-72 hours after starting therapy in bulky, rapidly dividing tumors. Prevention is hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase.

cards.front: How does malignant spinal cord compression present, and what is done first?
cards.back: Back pain worse at night and lying flat for weeks, then weakness, a sensory level, and late bladder and bowel dysfunction. Give dexamethasone immediately, then urgent MRI of the whole spine.

cards.front: What is superior vena cava syndrome, and what actually makes it an emergency?
cards.back: Facial and arm swelling with distended neck and chest veins, worse lying flat, from tumor obstructing the SVC. The emergency is airway edema or cerebral edema, not the swelling itself.

cards.front: What is hyperviscosity syndrome and how is it treated?
cards.back: Very high paraprotein or blast counts thicken blood, causing blurred vision, headache, mucosal bleeding and confusion. Treatment is plasmapheresis or leukapheresis.

cards.front: When is the neutrophil nadir after chemotherapy, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Typically 7-14 days after a cycle. That is when a single fever with an ANC under 500 becomes an oncologic emergency needing cultures and antibiotics within one hour.

cards.front: What four questions structure the approach to any rash?
cards.back: Is the patient sick? Does it blanch? What is the primary lesion — macule, papule, plaque, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal? Where is it and how is it distributed?

cards.front: Name the five rash red flags that mean escalate now.
cards.back: Non-blanching rash with fever, mucous membrane involvement, skin painful to touch, skin that sloughs, and any rash spreading over hours.

cards.front: Which rashes must be recognized in a febrile, ill-appearing patient?
cards.back: Non-blanching purpura suggests meningococcemia; wrist and ankle spots moving inward after a tick suggest Rocky Mountain spotted fever; sloughing skin with eroded lips suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome or TEN.

cards.front: How do erysipelas, cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis differ on inspection?
cards.back: Erysipelas is a sharply demarcated raised bright red plaque. Cellulitis is warm spreading redness with no sharp edge. Necrotizing fasciitis looks mild but hurts severely, with crepitus and a toxic patient.

cards.front: Describe the appearance of shingles, chickenpox and hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
cards.back: Shingles: grouped painful vesicles in one dermatome stopping at the midline. Chickenpox: crops of vesicles at different stages. Hand, foot and mouth: vesicles on palms, soles and in the mouth of a toddler.

cards.front: Give the ABCDE criteria and the ugly duckling rule.
cards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving. The ugly duckling is the mole that looks unlike the patient's other moles, and it is often the most useful sign.

cards.front: How do basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma look and behave?
cards.back: Basal cell: pearly translucent papule with fine vessels and a rolled edge, locally destructive, almost never metastasizes. Squamous cell: firm scaly or ulcerated nodule on lip, ear, scar or chronic wound, and it can metastasize.

cards.front: Which melanoma is most often missed in darker skin?
cards.back: Acral lentiginous melanoma, appearing on palms, soles and under nails. It is proportionally more common in darker-skinned patients and is frequently mistaken for a bruise or fungal nail change.

cards.front: How does timing separate the drug eruptions?
cards.back: Urticaria in minutes to hours, morbilliform at 4-14 days, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and TEN at 4-28 days, DRESS at 2-8 weeks, and AGEP at 1-3 days. Culprits: sulfonamides, penicillins, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs.

cards.front: What defines hyperemesis gravidarum and what must be given before dextrose?
cards.back: Persistent vomiting with over 5% weight loss, ketonuria and electrolyte derangement. Give thiamine before any dextrose-containing fluid, because a glucose load can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

cards.front: When is gestational diabetes screened, and what are the consequences?
cards.back: Screened at 24-28 weeks with a 50 g challenge then a 100 g tolerance test. It causes macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia and preeclampsia, and about half of women develop type 2 diabetes within a decade.

cards.front: What are the severe features of preeclampsia?
cards.back: Blood pressure 160/110 or higher, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 mg/dL or doubled, transaminases at twice normal, pulmonary edema, or new headache or visual disturbance.

cards.front: Give the magnesium sulfate regimen and how toxicity is recognized and treated.
cards.back: 4-6 g IV load over 20 minutes then 2 g/hr. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output; lost reflexes are the first sign of toxicity, treated with calcium gluconate 1 g IV.

cards.front: Which antihypertensives are used for severe-range pressure in pregnancy, and what is the target?
cards.back: Labetalol 20 mg IV, hydralazine 5-10 mg IV, or immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg orally. The target is 140-150/90-100, not a normal pressure, because placental perfusion depends on it.

cards.front: How do placenta previa and placental abruption differ?
cards.back: Previa: painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus, and no digital or speculum exam until ultrasound excludes it. Abruption: painful bleeding with a rigid tender uterus, fetal distress, possible concealed bleeding and DIC.

cards.front: What are the four Ts of postpartum hemorrhage?
cards.back: Tone, meaning uterine atony and 70-80% of cases; Trauma from lacerations or inversion; Tissue from retained placenta; and Thrombin, meaning coagulopathy.

cards.front: Give the postpartum hemorrhage treatment ladder with doses and cautions.
cards.back: Massage and empty the bladder, oxytocin 10-40 units in 1 L, tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours, then methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM (not in hypertension) or carboprost 250 mcg IM (not in asthma), then balloon tamponade, embolization, surgery.

cards.front: Name the postpartum emergencies besides hemorrhage.
cards.back: Endometritis with fever, uterine tenderness and foul lochia; postpartum preeclampsia or eclampsia up to 6 weeks out; amniotic fluid embolism with collapse, hypoxia and DIC; and postpartum psychosis.

cards.front: Give the first-line treatments for chlamydia, gonorrhea and early syphilis.
cards.back: Chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, or azithromycin 1 g once in pregnancy. Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once. Early syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once.

cards.front: What is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction?
cards.back: Fever, chills and a worsening rash within 24 hours of treating syphilis, caused by dying organisms releasing their contents. It is not a penicillin allergy and does not contraindicate continuing treatment.

cards.front: What are the partner and follow-up rules after a sexually transmitted infection?
cards.back: Treat partners from the last 60 days, abstain from sex for 7 days after treatment and until partners are treated, and retest at 3 months. Test of cure is only for pregnancy and pharyngeal gonorrhea.

cards.front: What is expedited partner therapy?
cards.back: Providing treatment for a partner who has not been examined, permitted for chlamydia and gonorrhea in most states including New Jersey. It reduces reinfection when partners will not present for care.

cards.front: Rank contraceptive methods by typical-use failure rate.
cards.back: Implant and IUDs under 1%, injection about 4%, pill, patch and ring about 7%, male condoms about 13%, withdrawal about 20%. Long-acting methods win because they do not depend on the user.

cards.front: When is estrogen-containing contraception contraindicated?
cards.back: Migraine with aura, prior venous thromboembolism or thrombophilia, smoking at age 35 or older, uncontrolled hypertension, current breast cancer, and the first 21 days postpartum. Progestin-only methods remain available.

cards.front: Compare the emergency contraception options.
cards.back: Copper IUD is over 99% effective up to 5 days and continues as contraception. Ulipristal 30 mg works to 120 hours and holds up better at higher weight. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg works to 72 hours. All delay ovulation.

cards.front: How do testicular torsion and epididymitis differ, and what are the salvage rates?
cards.back: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex, no relief with elevation. Epididymitis: gradual, with fever and dysuria, eased by elevation. Salvage nears 90% within 6 hours and falls under 10% past 24.

cards.front: Name three other male genitourinary emergencies and their time pressure.
cards.back: Ischemic priapism over 4 hours is a compartment syndrome needing aspiration and phenylephrine. Paraphimosis needs compression and reduction now. Fournier gangrene is perineal necrotizing fasciitis needing emergency debridement.

quiz.q: A patient has a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL with an absolute reticulocyte count of 210,000/microliter. What does this indicate?
choices: The marrow is responding, so the cause is destruction or blood loss
The marrow is failing to produce red cells
The result is inconsistent with anemia
quiz.why: A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is compensating, which points to hemolysis or bleeding. Underproduction states such as iron deficiency or chronic disease show an inappropriately low reticulocyte count.

quiz.q: Which iron study pattern fits anemia of chronic disease rather than iron deficiency?
choices: Low ferritin with high total iron binding capacity
Normal or high ferritin with low total iron binding capacity
Low ferritin with low transferrin saturation and a high RDW
High ferritin with a high red cell count
quiz.why: Inflammation traps iron in storage, so ferritin is normal or high while transport capacity falls. Iron deficiency does the opposite, with a low ferritin and a high binding capacity.

quiz.q: A 29-year-old woman has been taking iron for 6 months for microcytic anemia with no improvement. Her ferritin is 140 ng/mL, red cell count 6.1 million/microliter and RDW normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Small cells with a high red cell count, a normal RDW and a normal or high ferritin describe thalassemia trait, and continued iron risks overload. Persistent blood loss or non-adherence would leave ferritin low.

quiz.q: Which finding on a peripheral smear points to a microangiopathic process?
quiz.why: Schistocytes are red cells sheared apart in small vessels, seen in TTP, HUS, DIC and mechanical valves. Spherocytes suggest warm autoimmune hemolysis or hereditary spherocytosis, and hypersegmented neutrophils suggest megaloblastic anemia.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old man is found to have iron deficiency anemia with no obvious bleeding source. What is required?
choices: A 3-month trial of oral iron, then reassessment
Reassurance, since men lose iron through diet variation
quiz.why: Iron deficiency in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman implies gastrointestinal blood loss, and occult malignancy must be excluded with both scopes. Replacing iron without investigating misses the cancer.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old boy has a swollen painful knee after minor trauma, with a prolonged PTT and a normal PT and platelet count. What is the likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Bleeding into a joint with an isolated prolonged PTT in a boy is hemophilia. Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding, ITP lowers platelets, and vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT first.

quiz.q: A known severe hemophiliac struck his head 40 minutes ago and is neurologically normal. What should happen first?
choices: CT head, then factor if bleeding is seen
Observation for 4 hours with serial exams
Give factor concentrate now, then image
Check a PTT and decide based on the result
quiz.why: Factor replacement is time-critical and is given before imaging, because a normal exam does not exclude an expanding bleed and the CT costs time that cannot be recovered. The PTT does not guide acute dosing.

quiz.q: A 17-year-old girl has had heavy periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds and easy bruising, with a normal platelet count and a mildly prolonged PTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelets and a mildly prolonged PTT fits von Willebrand disease, which is autosomal and affects women equally and also carries factor VIII. Hemophilia is X-linked and causes deep bleeding.

quiz.q: A patient with TTP has a platelet count of 11,000/microliter. What must be avoided?
choices: Platelet transfusion for the low count alone
Red cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia
quiz.why: Transfused platelets are consumed by the ongoing microthrombotic process and can worsen organ ischemia. Plasma exchange is the treatment, steroids are adjunctive, and red cells may be given for anemia.

quiz.q: A patient on heparin for 7 days has a platelet count that fell from 240,000 to 90,000, with a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the correct action?
choices: Stop all heparin and start argatroban
Change to low molecular weight heparin
