quiz.why: This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a prothrombotic state, so every heparin source including flushes and low molecular weight forms must stop and a non-heparin anticoagulant started. Platelets are not transfused.

quiz.q: In DIC with active bleeding, which product corrects a fibrinogen of 90 mg/dL?
quiz.why: Cryoprecipitate is the concentrated source of fibrinogen and is used when fibrinogen falls below 150 mg/dL. Plasma supplies all factors but in a volume that may not raise fibrinogen adequately.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has a heart rate of 130 and a systolic pressure of 84 mmHg with ongoing bleeding. What does the shock index indicate?
choices: It is normal at this heart rate
It suggests compensated shock needing only crystalloid
It cannot be calculated without a hemoglobin
It exceeds 1, a trigger to activate massive transfusion
quiz.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, here about 1.5, and a value above 1 is a recognized trigger to activate the protocol before formal criteria are met. Crystalloid alone dilutes and cools.

quiz.q: What ratio of products is used in a massive transfusion protocol?
choices: Red cells alone until the hemoglobin reaches 10
Plasma alone until the INR normalizes
quiz.why: A balanced 1:1:1 ratio approximates whole blood and avoids diluting clotting factors and platelets. Red-cell-heavy resuscitation produces a dilutional coagulopathy.

quiz.q: A patient bleeding after a motor vehicle crash arrives 90 minutes after injury. What is true about tranexamic acid?
choices: It is no longer useful after 60 minutes
It should be given now, within the 3-hour window
It should be withheld until the INR is known
It is contraindicated with blood products
quiz.why: Tranexamic acid reduces mortality when given within 3 hours of injury, as 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours. Given later it does not help, and it is used alongside blood products, not instead of them.

quiz.q: Ten minutes into a transfusion a patient has a fever of 39.1 C, flank pain, dark urine and a blood pressure of 78/44. After stopping the transfusion, what matters most?
choices: Give an antipyretic and restart slowly
Send the patient for a chest radiograph
Aggressive isotonic fluids to protect the kidneys, and recheck identifiers
Give a diuretic for the dark urine
quiz.why: This is an acute hemolytic reaction, almost always an identification error, and free hemoglobin injures the kidneys unless urine output is maintained. Restarting the unit would be lethal and a diuretic worsens perfusion.

quiz.q: Which transfusion hazard is now the most likely infectious risk?
quiz.why: Viral transmission risk is now roughly 1 in a million units or less because of nucleic acid testing, while platelets stored at room temperature can grow bacteria. That makes bacterial contamination the leading infectious hazard.

quiz.q: A competent adult refuses all blood transfusion before an operation with expected blood loss. What is the correct approach?
choices: Honor the refusal, ask which products and techniques are acceptable, and plan iron, TXA and cell salvage
Transfuse anyway if the hemoglobin falls under 7 g/dL
Obtain a court order before proceeding
quiz.why: A competent adult's refusal is binding, and the useful work is making it specific, since many patients accept albumin, factor concentrates or cell salvage. Court involvement applies to minors, not competent adults.

quiz.q: A patient exposed 12 days ago has a fever, rash and sore throat, and a negative HIV antibody-antigen screen. What is the best next test?
choices: Repeat the antigen-antibody test in 6 weeks only
quiz.why: Acute HIV presents before antibodies form, and the RNA test detects virus from about 10 days. Waiting 6 weeks leaves a highly infectious patient untreated, and a CD4 count does not diagnose infection.

quiz.q: An HIV-positive patient has a CD4 count of 160 cells/microliter. What prophylaxis is indicated?
choices: No prophylaxis until the CD4 falls under 100
quiz.why: Pneumocystis prophylaxis begins at a CD4 under 200 and TMP-SMX is the agent of choice. Toxoplasmosis coverage matters under 100 and is provided by the same drug, and MAC prophylaxis was historically used under 50.

quiz.q: A patient starting antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 of 45 develops fever and enlarging lymph nodes 3 weeks later, with a falling viral load. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: A new opportunistic infection requiring therapy to stop
quiz.why: A recovering immune system inflames a previously silent infection, so the patient looks worse while the viral load falls. Treatment failure would show a rising viral load, and antiretroviral therapy is usually continued through IRIS.

quiz.q: A patient requests PrEP. What must be confirmed before starting?
choices: A negative HIV test, with repeat testing every 3 months
quiz.why: Starting two-drug PrEP during undiagnosed HIV infection breeds resistance, so a negative test is required before starting and every 3 months thereafter. PrEP is not contraindicated in pregnancy.

quiz.q: A man steps on a rusty nail through his shoe. He completed a primary tetanus series as a child and had a booster 7 years ago. What does he need?
choices: Nothing, since the wound is minor
quiz.why: A dirty or contaminated wound requires a booster if the last dose was more than 5 years ago, and 7 years qualifies. Immune globulin is added only when fewer than three lifetime doses were given or the history is unknown.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old woman has a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, pleuritic chest pain and a positive ANA. Which result would best support lupus specifically?
quiz.why: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for lupus, while ANA is sensitive but common in healthy people. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP belong to rheumatoid arthritis and HLA-B27 to spondyloarthritis.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old has 3 weeks of new one-sided headache, pain in the jaw after a few bites of food, and brief visual blurring. ESR is 88 mm/hr. What is the most important next step?
choices: Schedule temporal artery biopsy for next week
Obtain MRI of the brain first
quiz.why: Vision loss in giant cell arteritis is sudden and permanent, and the biopsy remains diagnostic for about two weeks after steroids start. Delaying treatment for imaging or tissue risks irreversible blindness.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old man has 8 months of back pain that is worst after rest, wakes him at 4 a.m., and improves with exercise. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Inflammatory back pain, suggesting ankylosing spondylitis
quiz.why: Pain worse with rest and better with activity, with night waking and prolonged morning stiffness, is inflammatory. Mechanical pain and disc disease are worse with activity and better with rest.

quiz.q: A pathology report describes a poorly differentiated tumor with no nodal involvement and no metastasis. Which statement is correct?
choices: The grade is low and the stage is high
The grade is high and the stage is early
Grade determines whether metastases are present
quiz.why: Poor differentiation is a high grade, describing how abnormal the cells look, while absent nodes and metastases make the stage early. Grade and stage answer different questions and often diverge.

quiz.q: A patient on a checkpoint inhibitor develops 8 watery stools daily with abdominal cramping. What is the most likely cause and treatment?
quiz.why: Checkpoint inhibitors release immune brakes and produce autoimmune organ inflammation, of which colitis is among the most common, treated with steroids. Infection is excluded but antibiotics do not treat this mechanism.

quiz.q: Which electrolyte pattern defines tumor lysis syndrome?
choices: Low potassium, low phosphate, high calcium
High potassium, low phosphate, high calcium
Low potassium, high phosphate, low calcium
High potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium
quiz.why: Lysing cells release potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids that become uric acid, and the phosphate binds calcium, driving it down. Kidney injury follows from urate and calcium phosphate deposition.

quiz.q: A woman with breast cancer has facial swelling, distended chest wall veins and a headache that worsens when she bends forward. What is this?
quiz.why: Obstruction of the superior vena cava by tumor produces upper body venous congestion that worsens when lying flat or bending forward. Angioedema is acute and asymmetric, and heart failure causes dependent edema.

quiz.q: A patient with multiple myeloma has blurred vision, headache, confusion and mucosal bleeding with a very high protein level. What treatment is needed?
quiz.why: Hyperviscosity from a high paraprotein impairs microcirculation, and plasmapheresis physically removes the protein. Transfusing red cells actually raises viscosity and can worsen the syndrome.

quiz.q: A rash is being assessed. Which single bedside maneuver most quickly separates dangerous from benign causes?
choices: Pressing on it to see whether it blanches
quiz.why: Non-blanching means blood has left the vessels, which in a febrile patient signals meningococcemia or another serious process. Size, itch and family history rarely change immediate management.

quiz.q: A patient started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 10 days ago and now has painful skin, eroded lips and conjunctivae, and sheets of epidermis shearing off with gentle pressure over 25% of the body. What is this?
quiz.why: Painful skin with mucosal erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and extensive detachment is toxic epidermal necrolysis, requiring burn-unit care. A morbilliform eruption does not involve mucosa or cause sloughing.

quiz.q: A hiker has an expanding round red patch on the thigh with slight central clearing, 9 days after a camping trip. What does this represent?
choices: Erythema migrans of early Lyme disease
quiz.why: An expanding annular patch after outdoor exposure is erythema migrans, which is treated empirically without waiting for serology, since antibodies may not have formed. Tinea has a scaling edge and cellulitis is warm, tender and not annular.

quiz.q: A patient's leg is only mildly erythematous but he is in severe pain, has a heart rate of 130, a temperature of 39.2 C, and crepitus on palpation. What is the priority?
choices: Intravenous antibiotics and admission for cellulitis
Immediate surgical consultation for necrotizing fasciitis
Doppler ultrasound for deep vein thrombosis
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion to appearance with crepitus and systemic toxicity is necrotizing infection, and survival depends on early debridement. Antibiotics alone do not reach devitalized fascia.

quiz.q: A dark-skinned patient has an irregular, evolving pigmented lesion under a thumbnail that has been growing for months. What should be considered?
quiz.why: Acral lentiginous melanoma arises on palms, soles and nail beds and is the form most often missed in darker skin, frequently mistaken for a bruise or fungal change. A hematoma grows out with the nail rather than expanding over months.

quiz.q: A woman at 10 weeks has vomited for 2 weeks, has lost 8% of her body weight and has ketonuria. She needs intravenous fluids. What must be given before dextrose?
quiz.why: A glucose load in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, which has occurred in hyperemesis. Thiamine goes in first, and antiemetics and electrolytes follow.

quiz.q: A woman at 36 weeks has a blood pressure of 176/116 and a headache. She receives magnesium, and 3 hours later her patellar reflexes are absent and her respiratory rate is 10. What should be given?
quiz.why: Absent reflexes followed by respiratory depression is magnesium toxicity, reversed with calcium gluconate while the infusion is stopped. Naloxone treats opioids and a further bolus would deepen the toxicity.

quiz.q: A woman at 32 weeks has heavy painless bright red vaginal bleeding with a soft non-tender uterus. What must not be done?
choices: Establish IV access and check maternal vital signs
Obtain an ultrasound to locate the placenta
quiz.why: Painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus suggests placenta previa, and any vaginal examination can provoke catastrophic hemorrhage until ultrasound excludes it. Access, monitoring and imaging are all appropriate.

quiz.q: A woman delivers and 20 minutes later has heavy bleeding with a soft boggy uterus. Massage and oxytocin have not worked, and her blood pressure is 158/98. Which agent should be avoided?
quiz.why: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and is avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia. Carboprost is the one avoided in asthma, and misoprostol and tranexamic acid are safe here.

quiz.q: A woman collapses minutes after delivery with sudden hypoxia, hypotension and then oozing from every puncture site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Abrupt cardiorespiratory collapse around delivery followed by DIC is the classic amniotic fluid embolism picture. Atony causes visible uterine bleeding, eclampsia causes seizures, and endometritis develops over days with fever.

quiz.q: A non-pregnant 25-year-old tests positive for chlamydia. What is the preferred treatment?
choices: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
quiz.why: Doxycycline for 7 days is now preferred over single-dose azithromycin for genital chlamydia because of better cure rates. Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea and metronidazole treats trichomoniasis.

quiz.q: A pregnant woman with a documented penicillin allergy tests positive for syphilis. What is the correct management?
choices: Penicillin desensitization, then benzathine penicillin G
quiz.why: Only penicillin reliably prevents congenital syphilis, so an allergic pregnant patient is desensitized and then treated. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and deferral risks fetal infection.

quiz.q: A 33-year-old with migraine with aura wants reliable contraception. Which option is contraindicated?
quiz.why: Estrogen raises ischemic stroke risk in migraine with aura, so combined methods are avoided. Progestin-only and non-hormonal methods are all acceptable and more effective in typical use.

quiz.q: A 15-year-old has 4 hours of sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomiting. The left testis is high and horizontal, there is no cremasteric reflex, and elevation does not help. Ultrasound will take 90 minutes. What is the priority?
choices: Wait for ultrasound before calling anyone
Give analgesia and reassess in the morning
Call urology now; attempt manual detorsion while preparing for surgery
quiz.why: Salvage approaches 90% within 6 hours and collapses after 24, so surgical consultation cannot wait for imaging. Manual detorsion may restore flow temporarily but never replaces the operating room, and elevation relieving pain would have suggested epididymitis.

quiz.q: A man with sickle cell disease has a rigid, painful erection lasting 5 hours. What does this require?
choices: Urgent CT angiography of the pelvis
quiz.why: Ischemic priapism is a compartment syndrome of the penis, and permanent damage follows beyond a few hours, so decompression and phenylephrine are urgent. Non-ischemic priapism after trauma is the type that can be observed.

scenarios.title: Heavy bleeding forty minutes after delivery
scenarios.intro: A 31-year-old woman delivered a 9 lb 4 oz baby vaginally forty minutes ago after a long labor with oxytocin augmentation. The placenta was delivered intact. She is now soaking through pads, there is a steady trickle of blood, and the nurse's hand on her abdomen reports the uterus feels soft and high. Estimated loss so far is about 900 mL and climbing.

steps.prompt: She is pale and anxious. Before choosing a drug, what is done first?

choices.text: Firm bimanual uterine massage, empty the bladder, second large-bore IV, and call for help
choices.feedback: Correct. Atony causes 70-80% of postpartum hemorrhage, and massage with an empty bladder is both diagnosis and treatment. Access and help are summoned at the same moment, not after.

choices.text: Send a complete blood count and wait for the hemoglobin before acting
choices.feedback: The hemoglobin lags behind acute whole blood loss and will not change what the uterus needs. Treat the soft uterus in front of you.

choices.text: Place the patient in Trendelenburg position and observe for 15 minutes
choices.feedback: Positioning does not contract a uterus, and 15 minutes of atony at this rate is several hundred more milliliters.

steps.prompt: The uterus firms slightly with massage but bleeding continues. Which medication comes first?

choices.text: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM
choices.feedback: This is a reasonable second-line agent, but oxytocin is first and her blood pressure must be checked before any ergot is given.

choices.text: Oxytocin 10-40 units in 1 L of crystalloid as an infusion
choices.feedback: Correct. Oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic and is run as a dilute infusion rather than pushed, which can cause hypotension.

choices.text: Carboprost 250 mcg IM immediately
choices.feedback: Carboprost is effective but second line, and it must be screened against asthma first. Start with oxytocin.

steps.prompt: It is now 70 minutes since delivery and bleeding persists at about 1600 mL total. What should be added, and what must be checked before the next uterotonic?

choices.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV, and check her blood pressure and asthma history before methylergonovine or carboprost
choices.feedback: Correct. TXA reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of delivery, and the second-line uterotonics each have a contraindication worth one question: hypertension for methylergonovine, asthma for carboprost.

choices.text: Give both methylergonovine and carboprost together without further questions
choices.feedback: Stacking agents without screening is how a hypertensive patient gets an ergot or an asthmatic gets a prostaglandin. Ask the two questions; they take seconds.

choices.text: Hold further drugs and move straight to the operating room
choices.feedback: Surgery may be needed, but medical management and TXA continue on the way there rather than being abandoned.

steps.prompt: She has now lost roughly 2200 mL. She is cold to touch, and the blood bank asks how you want products.

choices.text: Activate massive transfusion for 1:1:1 products, use a fluid warmer, and check ionized calcium
choices.feedback: Correct. Balanced products prevent dilutional coagulopathy, warming protects clotting enzymes, and citrate in stored blood will drop her ionized calcium during rapid transfusion.

choices.text: Give 3 L of room-temperature crystalloid and red cells only
choices.feedback: Crystalloid cools and dilutes, and red cells alone leave her without clotting factors or platelets. This is how the lethal diamond assembles.

choices.text: Transfuse red cells and wait for coagulation results before ordering plasma
choices.feedback: Waiting for labs in an active massive hemorrhage means the plasma arrives after the coagulopathy is established. Protocols exist precisely to skip that delay.

steps.prompt: Products are running and she is warmer. Uterotonics have not controlled the bleeding, and the uterus is still boggy.

choices.text: Intrauterine balloon tamponade now, with interventional radiology and surgery mobilized
choices.feedback: Correct. When drugs fail, the ladder moves to mechanical control: balloon tamponade, then uterine artery embolization, then surgery. Escalation continues while products run.

choices.text: Repeat the full sequence of uterotonics from the beginning
choices.feedback: Drugs that have already failed at adequate dose will not work on a second pass, and the time spent is measured in blood.

choices.text: Continue transfusing and reassess in an hour
choices.feedback: Transfusion replaces what is lost but does nothing to stop the loss. Source control is the only thing that ends this.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: postpartum hemorrhage is a four-T problem, and atony accounts for most of it, so the hands go on the uterus before any drug is chosen. The ladder is massage and an empty bladder, oxytocin as an infusion, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, then a second-line uterotonic screened against hypertension and asthma, then mechanical control. Running underneath all of it is the transfusion physiology: balanced 1:1:1 products, a warm patient, and someone watching the ionized calcium that citrate is stripping away.

scenarios.title: Back pain in a man with lung cancer
scenarios.intro: A 64-year-old man with known metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer comes in for two weeks of mid-back pain. He says it is worse at night and when he lies flat, and that it woke him the last three nights. This morning his legs felt heavy on the stairs. He was told last week it was probably muscular.

steps.prompt: He is comfortable sitting up, in no distress, and the pain is reproducible with percussion over the mid-thoracic spine. What does the history alone suggest?

choices.text: Musculoskeletal strain; treat with NSAIDs and follow up
choices.feedback: Mechanical pain is better at rest and at night. Pain that is worse lying flat and wakes the patient, in someone with known cancer, is the opposite pattern.

choices.text: Possible malignant spinal cord compression; examine strength, sensation, reflexes and bladder function now
choices.feedback: Correct. New back pain in a cancer patient is cord compression until imaging says otherwise, and the neurologic examination at this moment is the most important data point in the case.

choices.text: Vertebral osteomyelitis; order blood cultures and defer imaging
choices.feedback: Infection is worth considering, but he is afebrile with known metastatic disease, and either way the imaging cannot be deferred.

steps.prompt: Examination shows 4 out of 5 strength in both hip flexors, brisk patellar reflexes, and reduced sensation below the level of the umbilicus. He has not urinated since morning.

choices.text: Give dexamethasone now and arrange urgent MRI
choices.feedback: Correct. Steroids reduce cord edema while imaging is arranged, and neurologic function at the time treatment starts is the best predictor of whether he walks afterward.

choices.text: Order MRI first and give steroids only if compression is confirmed
choices.feedback: Steroids are given on clinical suspicion because the delay for imaging is exactly the window in which function is lost. The scan does not become less useful for having treated first.

choices.text: Order plain radiographs of the thoracic spine
choices.feedback: Plain films cannot see the cord and a normal film does not exclude compression. They delay the study that matters.

steps.prompt: The radiologist asks which levels to image, given the sensory level at the umbilicus suggests roughly T10.

choices.text: Thoracic spine only, centered on T10
choices.feedback: A focused study risks missing a second lesion, and multiple levels of epidural disease are common in metastatic cancer.

choices.text: The entire spine, cervical through sacral
choices.feedback: Correct. Multi-level compression is common, and finding only the symptomatic lesion leads to treating one level while another progresses silently.

choices.text: Lumbar spine, since he has urinary retention
choices.feedback: Urinary retention here is a late sign of cord compression, not localization. A sensory level at the umbilicus points well above the lumbar spine.

steps.prompt: MRI shows epidural tumor compressing the cord at T9-T10 and a second smaller deposit at C6 without cord contact. A bladder scan shows 640 mL.

choices.text: Place a urinary catheter, continue dexamethasone, and involve radiation oncology and neurosurgery urgently
choices.feedback: Correct. The retention needs immediate relief, the steroid continues, and definitive treatment is decompression, radiation, or both, decided together and quickly.

choices.text: Admit for observation and plan radiation as an outpatient next week
choices.feedback: The interval between weakness and irreversible paralysis is often days. Outpatient scheduling forfeits the window.

choices.text: Stop the dexamethasone now that imaging is complete
choices.feedback: The steroid is treating cord edema, not the scan. It continues until definitive treatment is under way.

steps.prompt: His family asks why this was not caught last week, when the pain was the only symptom.

choices.text: Explain plainly that back pain in a cancer patient is the early warning, and that pain usually precedes weakness by days to weeks
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the teaching point of the case and it is also an honest answer: the pain phase is the treatable phase, and it is the phase most often attributed to muscles.

choices.text: Tell them nothing could have been done earlier
choices.feedback: That is not true, and it forecloses a conversation the family is entitled to have. Earlier imaging at the pain stage changes outcomes.

choices.text: Avoid the question and redirect to the treatment plan
choices.feedback: Deflecting erodes trust at exactly the moment the family needs to understand what happens next.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: in a patient with known cancer, back pain that is worse at night and lying flat is malignant spinal cord compression until an MRI says otherwise. The sequence is examine, give dexamethasone on suspicion, image the whole spine because second lesions are common, and involve radiation oncology and neurosurgery the same day. Neurologic status at the moment of treatment predicts whether the patient walks again, and the pain-only phase that precedes weakness by days to weeks is the phase where that outcome is decided.

scenarios.title: Reasoning it out: hemoglobin 7.8, and what to order next
scenarios.intro: Work this as an algorithm, not as pattern matching. A 58-year-old woman is referred for fatigue. Her hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL. She has no chest pain, no shortness of breath at rest, and normal vital signs. Nobody has ordered anything else yet. Your task is to decide what each test is for before you order it.

steps.prompt: Which test should be ordered first, and what question does it answer?

choices.text: Reticulocyte count, to ask whether the marrow is responding
choices.feedback: Correct. The first fork is production versus destruction or loss. A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is compensating, so you look for hemolysis or bleeding rather than a deficiency.

choices.text: Ferritin, since iron deficiency is the most common anemia
choices.feedback: Ferritin is often useful but it answers only one branch. Ordering it first assumes an answer instead of asking the question.

choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy, since the hemoglobin is under 8
choices.feedback: Biopsy is far down the algorithm and is almost never needed for a straightforward anemia workup. Start with non-invasive tests that sort mechanism.

steps.prompt: The absolute reticulocyte count is 28,000/microliter, which is low. The MCV is 74 fL. Which branch are you on?

choices.text: Underproduction with microcytosis: iron deficiency, thalassemia trait, or anemia of chronic disease
choices.feedback: Correct. A low reticulocyte count with small cells narrows to three realistic possibilities, and iron studies plus the red cell count separate them.

choices.text: Hemolysis, so order LDH and haptoglobin
choices.feedback: Hemolysis drives the reticulocyte count up, not down. This result argues against it.

choices.text: B12 deficiency, so order methylmalonic acid
choices.feedback: B12 and folate deficiency produce large cells, not small ones. The MCV points the other way.

steps.prompt: Ferritin is 8 ng/mL, total iron binding capacity is high, transferrin saturation is 9%, RDW is high and the red cell count is low. What is the diagnosis, and what does it obligate you to do?

choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia; prescribe iron and recheck in 3 months
choices.feedback: The diagnosis is right and the plan is half-finished. In a postmenopausal woman this finding demands a search for the source before anyone talks about iron dosing.

choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia; replace iron and refer for upper and lower endoscopy
choices.feedback: Correct. Iron deficiency in a postmenopausal woman or an adult man is a gastrointestinal blood loss, often a cancer, until both scopes say otherwise.

choices.text: Thalassemia trait; no treatment needed
choices.feedback: Thalassemia trait has a normal or high red cell count, a normal RDW and a normal ferritin. Every one of those is against it here.

steps.prompt: She is asymptomatic at rest with normal vital signs and a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL. Should she be transfused?

choices.text: Yes, transfuse two units to reach 10 g/dL
choices.feedback: The threshold in a stable non-bleeding patient is 7 g/dL, and transfusing to an arbitrary number exposes her to risk with no benefit.

choices.text: No; she is above the threshold of 7 g/dL, stable, and this developed slowly
choices.feedback: Correct. Symptoms and rate of fall matter more than the number, and a chronically anemic patient compensates. Iron replacement, not transfusion, is the treatment for the cause.

choices.text: Transfuse only if her heart rate exceeds 120
choices.feedback: That rule would be far too late, and it is not the standard. The decision rests on the threshold, symptoms and the trajectory together.

steps.prompt: Change the case. Suppose instead the reticulocyte count had come back at 260,000/microliter with an MCV of 96 fL, an LDH of 680 U/L, an undetectable haptoglobin and schistocytes on the smear, with platelets of 19,000. What now?

choices.text: Iron studies and a 3-month iron trial
choices.feedback: This picture is destruction, not deficiency. Iron does nothing for cells that are being sheared apart.

choices.text: Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia: treat as a thrombotic microangiopathy and arrange urgent plasma exchange
choices.feedback: Correct. Schistocytes plus a low platelet count is TTP, HUS or DIC until proven otherwise, and TTP needs plasma exchange the same day. Platelets are withheld.

choices.text: Transfuse platelets to above 50,000 before anything else
choices.feedback: Transfusing platelets into a thrombotic microangiopathy feeds the microthrombi. It is the single most harmful reflex in this scenario.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: run anemia as an algorithm and each test earns its place. Reticulocyte count first to split production from destruction, MCV second to sort the underproduction lane, then iron studies with the red cell count and RDW to separate deficiency from thalassemia trait and chronic disease. Two rules sit on top of the algorithm and are worth more than the details: iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman means both endoscopies, and schistocytes with thrombocytopenia means a thrombotic microangiopathy that needs plasma exchange and never platelets.
